title: Modular optical fault-tolerant quantum computation via an interface between verified resources and online logical operations
authors: Kosuke Fukui, Takaya Matsuura, Yohji Chin, Shohei Kiryu, Takaya Hoshi, Kan Takase, Warit Asavanant
abstract: We introduce a factory--processor interface architecture for modular optical fault-tolerant quantum computation that separates code-dependent encoded-resource preparation from reusable online logical processing on a common Gaussian optical processor. Beyond encoded resources, the interface specifies logical outputs, code-to-mode mapping, measurement roles, frame updates, verification records, and resource-injection boundaries. As a concrete realization, we combine an offline verified Bell-resource factory based on a recursively concatenated $C_4$ code with physical Gottesman--Kitaev--Preskill (GKP) qubits with an online time-domain measurement-based quantum computation (MBQC) processor. Under the specified additive-displacement-noise model and fixed postselection policy, simulations support the finite-level logical Bell-error ordering $P_5<P_4<P_3<P_2$ at 12.25 dB of effective GKP displacement-noise quality, both with and without the prescribed additional post-injection displacement noise. At 15.6 dB and $L=2$, a separate fixed-sample evaluation gives one-sided 95$\%$ Clopper--Pearson upper bounds below $10^{-5}$ for both conditions under the binomial model. The interface supports address-tracked injection, transversal CNOT and logical Bell-measurement constructions, and logical SWAP and Hadamard constructions with tracked code permutations. Given advance resource preparation and sufficient routing parallelism, increasing the concatenation level expands parallel encoded-resource width without increasing the protected online sequence length of these constructions. These results identify a modular route to lower logical error rates while retaining a common Gaussian MBQC operation set with shallow online processing.
summary: This paper introduces a modular architecture for fault-tolerant quantum computation using optical systems. It defines a formal interface to separate the preparation of verified quantum resources (the 'factory') from the actual computation (the 'processor'). By combining GKP qubits with Gaussian MBQC, the authors show that this modular approach can suppress logical errors effectively while maintaining a common, shallow online processing set.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of building a modular, fault-tolerant quantum computation (FTQC) architecture for optical systems by cleanly separating resource preparation from online processing.
main_result: They demonstrate that a defined interface allows for the construction of logical operations with finite-level error suppression, achieving low logical error rates in simulations.
method: The authors propose a factory--processor interface architecture that manages the flow of verified encoded resources and classical control information between an offline resource preparation module and a reusable online Gaussian processor.
model_or_system: The system is based on optical quantum computation using Measurement-Based Quantum Computation (MBQC) on a Gaussian processor built from Continuous-Variable (CV) clusters, utilizing Gottesman--Kitaev--Preskill (GKP) qubits for encoding.
key_observables: Logical Bell-error ordering ($P_5 < P_4 < P_3 < P_2$), effective GKP displacement-noise (measured in dB), and logical error probabilities.
important_parameters: The concatenation level ($L$), the effective GKP displacement-noise quality (e.g., 12.25 dB), and the noise model (additive-displacement-noise).
main_assumptions: The architecture relies on a formal interface that tracks not only the resource state but also classical records like addresses, roles, and verification outcomes.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the modular FTQC architecture showing the offline factory supplying verified resources and classical records to the common Gaussian MBQC processor via the interface. Figure 2 details the MBQC platform using a quad-rail lattice (QRL) for 2D CV cluster states.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the modular interface, details the physical implementation using GKP qubits and MBQC, presents the theoretical framework for resource characterization (including soft-decision decoding via LLRs), and concludes with simulation results demonstrating error suppression.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it proposes a concrete, scalable blueprint for fault-tolerant quantum computation in an optical setting, directly addressing resource management and modularity, which are key challenges in quantum optics.
